patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] btrfs: fix double release of data space on failed direct IO COW write

version_history.subject: [PATCH] btrfs: fix double release of data space on failed direct IO COW write

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the Btrfs file system where data space is released twice when a direct IO COW write fails, leading to an underflow of bytes_may_use and potential warnings or clamping to zero. The fix involves recording the extent consumed by btrfs_reserve_extent() in dio_data and releasing only the remaining reserved data space from bytes_may_use on error paths. This patch can be applied to stable kernels later than v5.19, which rewrote the affected error path.

review_comments.summary: reviewer noted that on x86, shadow-stack PTEs have their ordinary write bit clear but pte_write() reports them writable due to shadow-stack instructions; this allows HMM to grant devices write access to the process's shadow stack, potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing protection

Thanks.  This?

On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a

potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH] mm/hmm: skip NUMA balancing on protnone faults
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Patch proposes to skip NUMA balancing on PROT_NONE faults, aiming to reduce GPU performance impact.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price (Meta)
review_comments.summary: Raised questions about the performance implications of mmu_notifiers in the presence of PROT_NONE faults, specifically whether the driver needs a global view of memory or just a subset.

review_comments.author: Alistair Popple
review_comments.summary: Clarified the process of GPU page table setup and mmu_notifier synchronization, explaining that the driver doesn't need a global view of memory but rather just a view of the memory it needs to access.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 2026-11-17 at 10:57 +1100, "Gregory Price (Meta)" <gourry@gourry.net> wrote...
> On 2026-11-17 10:24 +1100, Alistair Popple wrote:
> > On 2026-11-14 at 07:53 +1100, "Gregory Price (Meta)" <gourry@gourry.net> wrote...
> > > On 2026-11-13 21:43 +0100, David Hildenbrand (Arm) wrote:
> > > > On 11/13/26 21:34, Thomas Hellstrm wrote:
> > > 
> > > > I recall that John (cc) kept saying "GPUs and NUMA balancing is inherently
> > > > incompatible, you have to disable NUMA balancing".
> > > > 
> > > 
> > > If this is a NUMA-hotplugged GPU, then this is resolved by a private
> > > node, because this:
> > > 
> > > @@ -6404,6 +6404,9 @@ static vm_fault_t do_numa_page(struct vm_fault *vmf)
> > >         if (!folio || folio_is_zone_device(folio))
> > > 
> > > 
> > > changes to
> > > 
> > >         if (!folio || folio_is_common_memory(folio))
> > > 
> > > And all folios on the GPU node are never subject to NUMA Balancing
> > > 
> > > so balancing can stay enabled while the GPU memory is not subject to
> > > PROT_NONE spew.
> > 
> > Hi Gregory, just to hopefully help clarify understanding a bit here this isn't
> > related to folio location and therefore private node won't help much.
> > 
> > This about a driver getting a snapshot of current PTE state to program a
> > secondary MMU (in this case on a GPU, but can equally be a NIC or other device).
> > 
> > Even CPU memory being subject to NUMA balancing can have quite an adverse impact
> > on GPU performance due to increased incidence of GPU faults, hence why John says
> > GPUs (using SVM) are inherently incompatible with NUMA balancing.
> > 
> 
> Ah, I follow.  I'm still working through the performance implications of
> mmu_notifiers in the presence of PROT_NONE faults, but if i'm
> understanding correctly it tracks that you'd say it's incompatible.

Incompatible is probably not the correct term as it still works. It's just that
GPU faults are really expensive, and to be avoided at all costs. So having NUMA
balancing running around randomly unmapping pages the GPU is using (regardless
of whether or not they are on the device) results in more GPU faults and
therefore a huge perf impact for basically no (or in fact sometimes negative)
gain.

> I presume here the driver needs a global view of memory (or at least all
> memory it can potentially DMA), rather than simply just a subset
> (some set of VMAs)?

The basic process is this:

* GPU needs to access some user space virtual address (eg. allocated with mmap/malloc)
* Therefore GPU driver needs to setup GPU page tables to point to the physical
  memory[1] backing the user space virtual address
* To find the physical address the GPU driver uses hmm_range_fault() on the
  range, possibly faulting pages in if required (ie. if CPU PTE permissions
  don't match what's required).
* hmm_range_fault() relies on mmu_notifiers for synchronisation with CPU PTE state.
* An mmu_notifier firing causes a driver to do two things:
  a) Must invalidate any GPU page tables / TLBs mapping the notified virtual address.
  b) Increments a sequence number for any concurrent hmm_range_faults(), which must
     retry as their view of CPU PTEs is now out-dated. This is the problem
     this patch series hits - the migration on fault causes an mmu_notifier to fire
     resulting in a hmm_range_fault() retry and associated overhead.

So the driver doesn't need a global view of memory, just a view of the memory
the GPU needs, or likely needs, to access. Determining that depends on the
driver - some might require pre-registration of the ranges (eg. via an ioctl)
prior to launching work whilst others might wait until the GPU work faults on an
address not in the GPU page tables. Or some combination thereof.

 - Alistair

[1] - Well technically the IOVA / DMA address mapping physical system memory
but that's not relevant for this discussion. We can assume there are no IOMMUs
present.

> ~Gregory
> 
> -- 
> ~Gregory
> 
>

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH RFC] NFS: don't wait for writeback on close() with a write delegation

version_history.subject: [PATCH RFC] NFS: don't wait for writeback on close() with a write delegation

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NFS client to no longer wait for writeback on close() when a write delegation is held, reverting behavior introduced by commit 5445b1fbd123. The change was made because waiting for writeback on close() provided no benefits and could lead to issues such as delayed error reporting and unnecessary flushing of data. Instead, the patch returns to the previous behavior where writeback is started on close() only when a write delegation is held. This change improves performance in certain scenarios, specifically single-threaded create/write/close operations against an NFS server with a nonzero space limit.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/4] mm: zswap: fix shrinker count for the root memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the zswap shrinker, which incorrectly scales the number of freeable entries on the root memcg's zswap LRU by its compression ratio. The issue arises because the root memcg's stats do not account for its own zswap entries, leading to incorrect scaling and potential data loss. The patch uses the zswap pool-wide counters instead, ensuring that all zswap entries are accounted for.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/4] mm: memcg: read root lruvec stats from the node counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series modifies the way root memcg's lruvec stats are read, allowing for more accurate and up-to-date statistics by reading from node counters instead of rstat values in certain cases.

review_comments.author: Chris Down
review_comments.summary: Identified potential issues with the allowlist approach, suggesting that the changelog should specify which stats are on the list. Also pointed out a specific stat (NR_VMSCAN_WRITE) that may need to be added to the list.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Joanne,

Joanne Koong writes:
>The exceptions are the kernel memory stats (slab, kernel stack, page
>tables, secondary page tables and vmalloc), hugetlb, and
>WORKINGSET_NODERECLAIM, which counts reclaimed xarray nodes (slab
>objects). Their node counters also count memory that isn't charged to a
>memcg, which falls into two categories:

This still describes the v2 denylist. With the allowlist, the root memcg
also keeps reading rstat for NR_ANON_MAPPED, NR_FILE_MAPPED, NR_SHMEM et
al, and some of those differ for reasons outside the two categories here,
like swapcache being counted differently in the node counter, for
example. Could the changelog say what is on the list instead? So that
would be the stats that only change through mod_lruvec_state(), with
everything else still reading rstat.

>+	case PGROTATE_ANON:
>+	case PGROTATE_FILE:
>+	case PGREFILL:
>+		return true;

NR_VMSCAN_WRITE isn't on the list, but prepare_scan_control() adds it to
WORKINGSET_RESTORE_ANON, so once the root flush in reclaim goes away,
root reclaim would mix a live node counter with a stale rstat value.
Unless I'm mistaken it should go here as well.

Once those are fixed, please feel free to add:

Reviewed-by: Chris Down <chris@chrisdown.name>

Thanks!

Chris

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/4] mm: workingset: skip the root memcg flush in workingset_test_recent()
series_items.patch_summary: The patch modifies the workingset_test_recent() function to skip flushing the root memcg's statistics when the eviction memcg is also the root memcg. This optimization avoids an expensive flush operation on the refault path, which can take up to 0.9ms in systems with high cgroup activity.

review_comments.summary: Recommended using a mem_cgroup_flush_lru_stats_ratelimited() helper to simplify the code and make it easier to understand. Acknowledged that skipping the root flush is acceptable, but suggested keeping the original patch's logic in mind for future changes.

Hi Joanne,

Joanne Koong writes:
>-	if (flush)
>+	if (flush && !mem_cgroup_is_root(eviction_memcg))

Not a big deal, but in the v2 thread you mentioned you would try a

and at least speaking for myself, keeping the root check close to the list

to hold this patch up though, and I've tested that refaults in the root

Tested-by: Chris Down <chris@chrisdown.name>

Thanks!

Chris

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm/page_alloc: drop unused gfp_mask from zone_watermark_fast()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes an unused argument from the zone_watermark_fast() function in the Linux kernel's page allocation module. The gfp_mask argument, which was introduced to check for atomic allocations, is no longer used since a previous commit switched the watermark boost check from __GFP_ATOMIC to ALLOC_MIN_RESERVE. The patch makes no functional changes and simply removes the unused argument.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm/page_alloc: move the kswapd node skip check into a helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the kswapd node skip check in the Linux kernel's page allocation code into a separate helper function called should_skip_kswapd_zone(). This makes the zone iteration cleaner and easier to read, while also resolving a checkpatch warning. The new function checks if kswapd is active on a node and if the zone is below its watermark for this request, and returns true if it should skip the zone. No functional changes are intended by this patch.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm/vmscan: consolidate promo vs. high watermark checks
series_items.patch_summary: This patch consolidates the pattern of checking the watermark that kswapd reclaims zones up to into a single helper function, reducing code duplication in three different sites. The function, `kswapd_wmark_pages`, takes into account whether NUMA balancing memory tiering is enabled and returns either the promo or high watermark accordingly. This change does not introduce any functional changes but simplifies the code by removing unnecessary includes and consolidating logic.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch set consists of three cleanups for the vmscan and page_alloc code, primarily aimed at making get_page_from_freelist easier to read. The changes include dropping an unused gfp_mask from zone_watermark_fast(), moving a kswapd node skip check into a helper function, and consolidating checks for promotion versus high watermark in vmscan. These cleanups are based on the latest page_alloc/for-next branch as of November 13, 2026, and do not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/3] mm/page_alloc: move the kswapd node skip check into a helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the kswapd node skip check in the Linux kernel's page allocation code into a separate helper function called should_skip_kswapd_zone(). This makes the zone iteration cleaner to read and resolves a checkpatch warning. The function checks if kswapd is active on a node and if the zone is below its watermark for the current request, and returns false if so. This prevents accidental 'node_reclaim_mode'-like behavior when another process has NUMA bindings causing kswapd wakeups on only some nodes. No functional change is intended by this patch.

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/compaction: do not skip the free scanner's periodic lock drop

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the isolate_freepages_block function in mm/compaction.c to fix a bug where the free scanner's periodic lock drop was being skipped when scanning pageblocks with strides above one. The issue arises because the scan steps over compound pages or high-order free pages, leading to potential deadlocks. To address this, the patch counts probes instead of pfns and checks every COMPACT_CLUSTER_MAX of them.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/3] mm: page_alloc: add a watermark check that knows the migratetype
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function __zone_watermark_ok_mt() to the Linux kernel's page allocation system, which takes into account the migratetype of the request when checking if an allocation can succeed. The function is used in several places where the caller needs to know whether the allocation will honor ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests. The patch also moves the declaration of __zone_watermark_ok() to mm/page_alloc.h and makes no functional changes yet, as it's a preparation for future changes that will make the high-order check respect ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/3] mm: page_alloc: make the high-order watermark check honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the high-order watermark check to honour the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag in page allocation. When defrag_mode is enabled, every slowpath allocation carries this flag, which prevents movable allocations from stealing free pages from other migratetype's blocks under memory pressure. The patch makes __zone_watermark_ok_mt() and __compact_finished() skip other migratetypes' free lists below pageblock_order for ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests, allowing compaction to run earlier and reducing stalls in compaction. This change is intended to fix issues with 64K mTHP faults under swap pressure.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/3] mm: vmscan: tell direct reclaim the allocation is ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the direct reclaim process in Linux to pass the allocation's flags down to try_to_free_pages(). Specifically, it records ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT in scan_control and uses this information to determine whether a costly order can succeed. This change is intended to improve performance by allowing direct reclaim to take advantage of free pages that are not movable or reclaimable. The patch was tested on Dev Jain's 64K mTHP benchmark and showed improved results, freeing more pages during direct reclaim with defrag_mode enabled.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses an issue where the high-order watermark check in the Linux kernel incorrectly counts free pages of every migratetype, leading to stalls and inefficiencies under memory pressure. The patches modify the watermark checks to honor the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag, which is set for slowpath allocations below pageblock_order. This change improves performance by preventing unnecessary compactions and direct reclaims, resulting in a significant reduction in 64K mTHP faults and improved overall system efficiency.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm/compaction: sample empty pageblocks again from a random offset

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/compaction: sample empty pageblocks again from a random offset

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's compaction algorithm to sample empty pageblocks from a random offset when the initial scan finds nothing. This is done to prevent aliasing issues that can cause free pages to be missed, particularly in sparse layouts or when memory is not aligned with the sampling grid. The change aims to improve the detection of free pages and reduce the likelihood of compaction failures, which can lead to stalled tasks and inefficient memory usage.

review_comments.author: Dev Jain
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Dev Jain questioned whether the patch's benefits would be observable in real workloads, citing low probabilities of missing free pages at random offsets and potential for unnecessary scans over fully filled memory.
review_comments.raw_body:
That is where it gets hairy: will this be observable in real workloads?

Suppose stride is 32 and the pageblock has 100 non-free pages. What is
the probability that 512 slots are filled with 100 objects such that
x = 0 (mod 32) is filled? It is

C(496, 84) / C(512, 100) = 1.6 *10^(-12), very improbable.

So the chance you have a sparse block and you are missing out by not
looking at other offsets is very low.

If stride = 32 and #objects = 400, the probability comes out to be
1.8%.

Keeping #objects fixed, lowering the stride lowers the probability
exponentially. (This is relevant since we start with lower strides)

On the other hand, what happens if you are scanning over fully filled
memory? (there is no way to tell whether a pageblock is sparse)
You are going to repeat the scans unnecessarily.

IOW I think the probability this patch is going to have a downside is
more than that of upside.

review_comments.author: Kiryl (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledged that their test case was not representative of real-world scenarios, but explained it was based on a bisection to identify the root cause of an issue in another series.
review_comments.raw_body:
Fair enough, let's drop it.

It is not entirely made up, though.

I stepped on it while testing another series. A fragmentation stress
test gave bimodal results: no direct reclaim in most runs and hundreds
to thousands of allocstalls in others.

It was confusing and looked like a regression in that series.

It took a bisection to find that the only thing that mattered was where
the free pages fell relative to the stride grid. The test in the
changelog was built after that, to show it on purpose.

The workload is very artificial, but the fix looked simple enough to
post.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 1/8] mm/gup: break out gup_fill_pages() helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch breaks out a helper function called `gup_fill_pages()` from the `__get_user_pages()` function in the Linux kernel's memory management code. The new helper function is responsible for storing consecutive pages into an array, and it is shared by both the slow and fast paths of the GUP (Get User Pages) operation. This change simplifies the code and reduces duplication, but does not introduce any functional changes. The patch also keeps a `pages==NULL` check in the helper function to handle cases where no pages array is passed.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 2/8] mm/gup: break out gup_flush_pages() helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch breaks out the cache flushing code from the __get_user_pages() function into a new helper function called gup_flush_pages(). The helper function takes in the number of pages and their addresses, and flushes each page's caches. This change is intended to improve code organization and maintainability without introducing any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 3/8] mm/gup: convert follow_page_mask() to return a long
series_items.patch_summary: This patch converts the return type of the follow_page_mask() function from a struct page pointer to a long integer. The new return value can be 0, a negative errno, or 1 with the found page stored in a pages[0] slot. This change allows the return type to carry a page count instead of a single struct page pointer.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 4/8] mm/gup: split out folio grab-and-store helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits the second part of the follow_page_pte function into a new helper called gup_grab_fill_folio_pages. This new function grabs a folio reference, marks it accessed and dirty if necessary, and stores the pages for the caller. The original function is simplified to only perform per-PTE safety checks. The cache flushes are moved to the caller's responsibility in __get_user_pages.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 5/8] mm/gup: break out gup_lookup_pte() helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch breaks out the gup_lookup_pte() helper from the larger follow_page_pte() function in mm/gup.c. The new helper resolves a present PTE to the page it maps, returning NULL if the PTE cannot be followed or a negative errno if the caller must report failure. This change is intended to simplify the code and improve maintainability without introducing any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 6/8] mm/gup: return a huge page's full count from follow_page_mask()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the follow_page_mask() function in the Linux kernel's mm/gup module to return the full count of huge pages instead of just a mask. It achieves this by removing unnecessary second-grab and subpage loop calls, and clamping the returned count to the huge page's size. The patch also removes dead code related to *page_mask and __get_user_pages()'s second-grab/subpage loop. The changes are intended to improve performance and simplify the code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 7/8] mm/gup: walk multiple PTEs per follow_page_pte() call
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the Linux kernel's memory management by allowing multiple PTEs (Page Table Entries) to be walked in a single call to follow_page_pte(). This reduces the number of page-table descents and lock acquisitions, resulting in improved performance. The patch also introduces a new approach for handling failures during the walk, where a failure on the first PTE is returned as before, but subsequent failures end the walk and allow __get_user_pages() to retry with an error. Measurements show significant improvements in get time over 16 iterations on a 256 MB MADV_HUGEPAGE region.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 8/8] mm/gup: batch contiguous same-folio PTEs into one refcount grab
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of large folios (mTHP) in the Linux kernel's memory management system by batching contiguous PTEs into one refcount grab, reducing the number of try_grab_folio() calls and improving performance. The patch introduces a new function gup_pte_batch_len() to determine how many PTEs can be committed as one run, and modifies the follow_page_pte() function to use this information. This change is particularly beneficial for large folios, where it reduces the time taken by 24.2 times compared to the previous implementation.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series improves performance in slow GUP (get user pages) by batching whole PTE tables and reducing the number of refcount grabs. The current slow path resolves and commits one PTE per call, leading to a restart of the page table descent and multiple refcount grabs for each page. This series brings the slow path up to speed with the fast path by introducing batch-length helpers and splitting out various functions to improve performance. The patches are reviewed in steps, starting with no-functional-change refactors and ending with the multi-PTE walk and same-folio batch commit. Measurements show a significant improvement in get time for large folios, with median times reduced by up to 12.8x.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm: mglru: splice all generations when reparenting a memcg

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm: mglru: splice all generations when reparenting a memcg

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a list_del corruption issue in the Linux kernel's memory management system (mm) by splicing all generations of MGLRU lists when reparenting a memcg (memory control group). The problem occurs when a memcg goes offline and its MGLRU lists are moved to the parent, but only certain generations are moved. This can lead to a folio being left on a freed memcg, causing a use-after-free error. To fix this, the patch moves all MAX_NR_GENS lists, not just those from min_seq to max_seq, ensuring that all folios are properly reparented and avoiding the corruption issue.

Reviewer noted that FG's folio_inc_lru_refs may cause a race between aging and lazy promotion, potentially landing a folio in a stall gen list, but agreed that this issue is not critical and can be addressed separately.

Thanks for looking into this!

FG needed that because FG's folio_inc_lru_refs is a generic MGLRU
lockless lazy promotion, it may cause race between aging & lazy
promotion, landing a folio in a stall gen list. This isn't a big
problem, the worst outcome is a hotness inversion, which happens
almost once in a million times.

And right as Shakeel pointed out the problem already exists for

---

review_comments.author: Yingjie Wang
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about root-cgroup charging and suggested that the increase may be due to boot-to-boot variation. Requested clarification in the changelog.
review_comments.raw_body:
> There is no kmem accounting in root cgroup, do you know why there is an increase
> of 2.3% there?

I think the 2.3% mainly reflects boot-to-boot variation. The unchanged
64-operation stack path also slowed down by 1.9%, even though it does
not reach the changed allocation.

For successful calls, the per-boot medians were:

  nops  V4 boots (ns)           V5 boots (ns)
  64    230.5 229.4 230.0       231.2 235.0 235.4
  65    546.0 551.2 548.2       551.2 562.6 566.3

The first V5 boot was very close to the upper end of the V4 results at
65 operations, while the later two boots were slower at both sizes.
That is why I interpret the increase mainly as boot-to-boot variation,
rather than root-cgroup charging.

__GFP_ACCOUNT does still change the allocation path, including selecting
the kmalloc-cg cache, so a small contribution from that is also possible.

Andrew, could we clarify the root-cgroup result in the [1/3] changelog?
Please change

  and successful calls in the root cgroup by at most 2.3%.

to

  and successful calls in the root cgroup by at most 2.3%, which
  appears to be mainly boot-to-boot variation.

Thanks,
Yingjie
